title: FloE: On-the-Fly MoE Inference on Memory-constrained GPU (Zhou*, Li*, Zhang, Wang, Wang, Xie, Chen, Shou; Zhejiang Univ. / Hangzhou High-Tech Zone Inst. of Blockchain and Data Security / UW). ICML 2025 (PMLR 267), arXiv 12 May 2025
id_read: arXiv 2505.05950v2 (PDF, pdftotext; first pass opened the v1 HTML; the numbers I checked are the same)
setup: Mixtral-8x7B only (47B total, 8 experts, top-2; every test case, footnote 3). Decode single batch, ShareGPT prompts, input/output lengths (32|64|128) x (128|256|512), mean of 5 runs. Hardware: one GeForce RTX 3090 24 GB, 64-core 2.3 GHz CPU, 256 GB DRAM, PCIe 4.0 (single-expert tests also on H100, A100, A6000). Baselines: DeepSpeed-MII (ZeRO-Infinity, FP16 offload), Mixtral-Offloading (dvmazur; expert cache + quantization), Fiddler (CPU-GPU co-execution), Mixtral-GPU (HQQ INT2 fully GPU resident, the upper reference). Method: gate/down projections sparsified by magnitude of the up-projection output (80-90% sparsity), up projection stored INT2 (HQQ), two predictors (learned inter-expert next-layer predictor; parameter-free intra-expert predictor that reuses the next layer's up-projection on the current hidden state), Triton sparse GEMV kernel (CATS-derived), compact column/row layout and AVX-512 multithreaded pinned-memory transfer. Accuracy: 7 lm-eval tasks (ARC-e, ARC-c, BoolQ, SciQ, OBQA, Winogrande, 5-shot MMLU) and WikiText-2.

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 91% of an INT2 GPU-resident Mixtral (a lossy reference), 95% max

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 4.4 and 7.6 are ABSOLUTE points on the 7-task average (72.0 -> 67.6 / 64.4); relative loss is 6.1% / 10.6%. 80% / 90% sparsity + INT2 up projection.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass: setting Mixtral-8x7B, RTX 3090
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: also 256 GB DRAM, PCIe 4.0, 12-24 GB VRAM sweep (Fig 8)

why: The mechanism that transfers is the idea itself: sparsify gate/down by |up-projection output| and predict the mask early by multiplying the previous layer's hidden state with the next layer's up matrix (hidden states of consecutive layers have cosine >0.95; intra recall 0.95). What breaks: (1) all speedups are PCIe DRAM-to-VRAM transfer savings on a 24 GB GPU with 256 GB DRAM; ours is CPU-only with weights on NVMe, so the saved bytes would be NVMe bytes, but the baseline is not DeepSpeed FP16 offload, it is already a 4.3-bit quantized layout with an LRU expert cache. (2) Up projection must be kept resident (INT2) or read in full, so at best 2/3 of the bytes are sparsified: gate-first/up-first caps byte saving at 1.5x for 50% (matches our pubtech/E.md gate-first cap). INT2 up projection is a quality loss we cannot take at 4.3 bits without our own test. (3) Mixtral has 8 experts of ~300 MB (FP16) with top-2; ours are 512 small experts, top-10 (a few MB each at 4.3 bits): sparsifying 80-90% of a few-MB expert leaves reads of ~0.3-0.5 MB, far below efficient NVMe read sizes (our E.md reads: 4 MiB 2.4 GB/s, 1 MiB 1.56 GB/s), so the compact layout trick matters but the read-size penalty is not measured by the paper. (4) The sparse magnitude threshold is calibrated on Mixtral, not on a 512-expert top-10 model, whose neurons may be less sparse. (5) Cache: FloE's best result needs cached layers in VRAM (Fig 8); our cache is 12-46% of the experts in RAM.
quality_loss: Yes, lossy: sparsity 80%/90% plus INT2 up projection gives -4.4 / -7.6 points average over 7 tasks (Fig 10); per task FloE-90% MMLU 53.1 vs 69.5 dense (-16.4 points; Fig 10 MMLU column). FloE-Wup-80% (without INT2) -2.7 points (69.3), FloE-Wup-90% -6.4 (65.6). For comparison (Fig 10): HQQ INT3 66.5, CATS-80% 65.7, CATS-90% 55.9, HQQ INT2 31.1. Authors note the MMLU drop from FloE-Wup to FloE is the largest.
ablation: Yes, partly: sparsity strategy (gate vs up vs down magnitude, Fig 3a/9a, up-projection chosen), quantization sensitivity per matrix (Fig 3b), sparse kernel alone (Table 1, up to 2x for the kernel), compact transfer alone (Fig 7, 12.6x), VRAM sweep 12-24 GB (Fig 8). There is no ablation separating predictor, sparsity and caching contributions to the end-to-end 2.6x, and no cache-size-as-share-of-experts isolation.
limitations: Authors do not include a limitations section. Stated scope: single-batch latency-sensitive decoding; all tests on Mixtral-8x7B (other models only for sensitivity in the appendix); when VRAM is sufficient raising up-projection bits recovers MMLU. Not stated: prefill/TTFT, batch >1, NVMe.
contradicts_our_findings: No contradiction. It agrees with our E.md closed form: with up kept dense the byte gain is capped (gate-first cap 1.5x at d=0.5), and sparse kernel speedup of the expert matmul is 1.43x at 50% (our compute-ceiling lift 1.17x at d=0.5 because dense share is fixed). It does not support the screen's 2.6x claim; the 2.6x in this paper is a different quantity (vs Mixtral-Offloading, includes INT2 and prediction).

title: Turbo Sparse: Achieving LLM SOTA Performance with Minimal Activated Parameters (Song, Xie, Zhang, Wen, Ma, Mi, Chen; IPADS SJTU, Tsinghua, Shanghai AI Lab). arXiv preprint, v2 11 Jun 2024
id_read: arXiv 2406.05955v2 (PDF); first pass read v1 HTML
setup: Mistral-7B and Mixtral-47B (8 experts, top-2) converted to dReLU (ReLU on both gate and up) by continued pretraining on ~150B tokens (diverse web/code/math mixture, Table 4) on 64 A800-80G, then SFT (predictors trained per expert during SFT). Small-scale study: 300M models, 5B tokens fineweb (dReLU vs SwiGLU). Speed: PowerInfer (sparse-aware) running TurboSparse models vs llama.cpp running the ORIGINAL dense-activation models. Hardware: PC-Laptop i9-14900HX 32 GB host RAM + RTX 4090 16 GB, PCIe 4.0; PC-2080Ti i7-12700K 64 GB + RTX 2080Ti 11 GB, PCIe 3.0; OnePlus 12 (Snapdragon 8 Gen 3, 24 GB DRAM, UFS 4.0) with PowerInfer-2. INT4 for Mixtral, FP16 for Mistral. Decode, batch 1.

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Table 9, 22.2x; 24 GB phone, UFS 4.0

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass: needs ~150B-token retraining; existing SwiGLU checkpoints stay ~40%
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 40% is the natural zero fraction. The paper's own Table 3 shows a SwiGLU model loses almost nothing at 50% top-k magnitude sparsity (28.48 -> 28.62 ppl) and degrades at 80% (36.28); Fig 5a shows Mixtral/DeepSeek-MoE/Qwen1.5-MoE lose ~1-2% average performance at 50% sparsity without any retraining.

why: (1) Requires the ReLU-fied checkpoint: ~150B training tokens, and every released 125B-class MoE we could run is SwiGLU, so we cannot get the 85-97% sparsity. (2) The speed comparison is against dense-activation llama.cpp on the same machine class and includes PowerInfer's predictors (per-expert neuron predictors trained in SFT), which cost memory (PowerInfer-2 measures 2.6 GB of predictors for the 47B). (3) Hardware is GPU+CPU PCs with 32-64 GB RAM holding a 47B INT4 model (~24 GB) - the model fits in RAM (Table 7 'CPU only' means RAM-resident), so there is no NVMe streaming in this paper; only the phone row streams (via PowerInfer-2). (4) Mixtral has 8 big experts; at 512 experts top-10 the sparse-FFN share is different. What does transfer: the observation (Fig 5a) that expert FFNs stay as sparse as dense FFNs (~50% prunable for ~1-2%).
quality_loss: Training-based: TurboSparse-Mixtral average 71.76 vs 69.34 original (Table 6), i.e. no loss (gain), but only after 150B tokens of continued pretraining plus SFT; contamination/mixture effects not isolated. Training-free sparsity on the original SwiGLU MoE (Fig 5a): about 1-2% average drop at 50% sparsity, steeper beyond 50% (no table, chart only).
ablation: Partial: dReLU vs SwiGLU at small scale (Tables 2-3), no ablation of predictor vs sparsity vs engine in the speed tables; no ablation of cache size.
limitations: Preprint under review, no limitations section. Sparsity measured as exact zeros on fineweb; predictor accuracy not reported in the paper; speed baselines run different checkpoints.
contradicts_our_findings: Consistent with E.md (TurboSparse needs ReLU-fication). One refinement: E.md says SwiGLU experts are 'only about 40% sparse until ReLU-fied'; the paper's Table 3 and Fig 5a show that magnitude-threshold sparsity of 50% is nearly free even on SwiGLU, which is the TEAL/CATS regime, not the 40% number.

title: PowerInfer-2: Fast Large Language Model Inference on a Smartphone (Xue*, Song*, Mi, Zheng, Xia, Chen; IPADS SJTU). arXiv v3 12 Dec 2024
id_read: arXiv 2406.06282v3 (PDF; pdftotext works, the first pass said the PDF was unreadable)
setup: Smartphones OnePlus 12 (24 GB DRAM, 19 GB usable, UFS 4.0, Snapdragon 8 Gen 3) and OnePlus Ace 2 (16 GB / 11 GB usable, UFS 3.1). Models: Mistral(SiLU)-7B, sparse Qwen2-7B, Bamboo-7B, sparse Llama-13B, TurboSparse-Mixtral-47B (INT4). Baselines: llama.cpp (mmap offload), LLMFlash re-implemented in llama.cpp (predictor, row-column bundling, neuron cache), QNN, MLC-LLM. FFN weights 50% in DRAM (75% offloaded for Mixtral on Ace 2). Decode prompts up to 64 tokens, 1024 output tokens, mean of 10 runs, batch 1 (BoN in 7.4). Method: neuron clusters as I/O/compute unit, gate-up-down neuron bundles (7.5 KB for INT4, 24 KB for FP16) read as one random read, segmented neuron cache (hot/cold), I/O-compute pipelining at cluster granularity, NPU for prefill/dense clusters, mlock via rooted Android.

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: UFS 4.0 single queue, 4 GB/s sequential; also model quality is not measured for the 47B in this paper (Table 7 only 7B models)

why: Transfers: the design principle that fits our regime is neuron-bundle reads (gate-up-down co-located, one random read per neuron bundle), cluster-level I/O/compute pipelining, and a segmented hot/cold cache; the ablation (Fig 14) shows bundle + cache + pipeline give 0.4 -> 9.6 tok/s on the phone. The 95% cache hit rate and 3.5% miss rate depend on the cache holding most of the activated neurons, because ReLU-fied TurboSparse activates only ~3B of 47B and 19 GB of 24 GB INT4 weights stay resident (about 75-80% of the model), whereas ours has 8-32 GB against a 69 GB model (12-46%) and SwiGLU. At 7 GB (1.8% cache of FFN) the system gets 2.13 tok/s, which is the closest to our 8 GB case, but it is a 47B with 3B active at 4 bits and 0.4-6 GB-class reads per token, vs our 125B with 6B active. Breaks: needs the sparse-trained model; NPU + CPU heterogeneity; UFS not NVMe; 2.6 GB of predictors; Android root.
quality_loss: PowerInfer-2 itself adds no extra loss beyond the sparse-model predictors, but the paper only measures accuracy on Bamboo-7B and Qwen2-7B (Table 7: -1.77 and -0.87 average points vs llama.cpp using group quantization) and not on TurboSparse-Mixtral-47B; 'negligible accuracy degradation' for the 47B is not shown here (TurboSparse paper reports no loss with retraining).
ablation: Yes (Fig 14, Bamboo-7B, 50% offload): bundling, neuron cache, pipeline, XPU each isolated; cache size sweep 7-19 GB (Fig 10) isolates memory. Layout (bundle) vs cache vs pipeline are separated, which is the useful part for us.
limitations: Not in a limitations section; the text notes the 47B at 9.96 tok/s still has room with a larger neuron cache, and UFS single command queue, 40% bandwidth loss under contention. Android root needed for mlock.
contradicts_our_findings: No contradiction; supports that cache size is the lever (decode speed scales linearly with memory up to 19 GB, Sec 7.2.3). Their finding that reads of a bundled 7.5 KB neuron unit work well on UFS (the cluster is small) is a data point our small-read penalty model (E.md: 35 KB block = 0.37 of large-read rate) did not include: they report bundling raising 0.4 -> 1.1 tok/s.

title: DualSparse-MoE: Coordinating Tensor/Neuron-Level Sparsity with Expert Partition and Reconstruction (Cai, Qin, He, Cui, Li, Huang; HKUST-Guangzhou, Univ. Maryland). arXiv v1 25 Aug 2025
setup: Training-free post-training system on SGLang. Models: Mixtral-8x7B (also Instruct and a fine-tuned 8->32 partitioned variant), OLMoE-Instruct (64 experts, top-8), DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat (64 routed top-6 + 2 shared). Hardware: server with 8x NVIDIA H20; Mixtral TP=8, OLMoE 1 GPU, DeepSeek EP=8. Speed test: 2000 random prompts, input 500 / output 100 tokens, batch size not stated (continuous batching in SGLang). Quality: lm-eval-harness on ARC-C, BoolQ, GSM8K(5-shot), HellaSwag, MMLU, OBQA, PIQA, RTE, WinoGrande. Method: split each expert into 'major' and 'minor' sub-experts by calibration importance of neurons (profiling on MMLU), then dual-threshold dropping on normalised gate score (below T_minor drop the whole token-expert pair, between thresholds compute major sub-expert only); load-aware thresholds per device.

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: correct in concept; no numbers in the catalog line

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: but the abstract headline numbers are 0.08-0.28% accuracy loss at ~25% drop and 1.41x / 1.13x with load-aware thresholding

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: not all on 8 GPUs: OLMoE single H20, Mixtral TP=8, DeepSeek EP=8

why: The gain is GPU computation and load balance in batched expert-parallel serving (grouped GEMM over many tokens per expert); the drop rate is measured over (token, expert) pairs and is translated into FLOP savings, not weight-read savings. With batch 1 and NVMe streaming, each token touches its own 10 experts and a dropped pair would save its bytes, so a gate-score threshold plus a major/minor split WOULD cut I/O in our regime, but (a) the paper does not test that, (b) the drop thresholds were calibrated on top-2/top-6/top-8 models (64 experts at most), and a 512-expert top-10 router has flatter gate scores, (c) our own k-reduction measurements (B.md, decode k=4 ~1.5x with unmeasured quality) cover the dynamic-drop idea, and the paper's contribution beyond that is the static major/minor neuron reordering (which would give the in-expert half-read). Quality results are on GPU-served instruct models with GSM8K the most sensitive task.
quality_loss: Yes (lossy, training-free): -0.08 (Mixtral fine-tuned), -0.28 (OLMoE), -0.18 (DeepSeek-V2-Lite) average points at ~22-27% token-expert drop, 9 tasks; 0.5% with load-aware thresholding at 1.41x; GSM8K the most sensitive task (they report GSM8K separately in Fig 11). 1T-Drop alone (no reconstruction) is worse on average.
ablation: Yes: 1T-Drop vs 2T (partition only) vs 2T (reconstruct) in Table 2 isolates the neuron-level reconstruction contribution; neuron importance metric ablation (accumulated gate / |gate| / gate-up / |gate-up|, DeepSeek avg 67.17/67.29/66.79/67.65, Sec 5.3.4); S-ETP communication only simulated/8xH20.
limitations: Authors state: calibration-sample dependence of neuron importance profiling, drop rate non-linear in threshold and varies by layer (per-layer thresholds left to future work), designed for distributed server-side inference rather than edge, MoE variants with more recent architectures remain future work.
contradicts_our_findings: No contradiction. Their EES row (skip second expert of top-2 when score below beta x first) is the same family as our decode-k-reduction rows; Table 3 gives a data point: EES -2.4% GSM8K at 1.05x, compared with our unmeasured-quality 1.4-1.7x k=4 byte gain.

why: Transfers as a CPU/NVMe-agnostic idea only: the 50% input-activation sparsity costs +0.4 ppl on quantized dense Llama, so reading half of each weight column would be nearly free quality-wise on dense models. Breaks: (1) Apple Metal GPU kernels, no CPU path (the paper says nothing about CPU or SSD). (2) Dense models only; no MoE experiment; MoE experts are small and the input hidden state to each expert is shared by 10 experts. (3) The skipped weights come from RAM-resident quantized weights; for NVMe-streamed experts, skipping columns requires column-contiguous quantization groups (their zigzag layout: groups along columns) which then fits exactly the bundle layout needed for partial reads; that part is a useful design observation. (4) Gain is 1.15-1.55x end to end at 50% because attention/embedding/etc. are not sparsified; prefill dense.
quality_loss: Perplexity only (no task benchmarks): Q4_K -> unified 50% sparsity +0.37 (Llama-2-7B), +0.74 (Llama-3-8B), +0.42 (Llama-2-70B); 65% is clearly worse (7.39 on 7B).
ablation: Yes: naive sparse in default layout (B1, slowdown), own layout without load balancing (B2), full; dense zigzag kernel vs default; sparsity 25/40/50/65%. No cache or I/O ablation (everything is RAM-resident).
limitations: Authors: preliminary work; dense GEMM/tiling for prefill not optimised, Apple GPUs only in the current implementation, Llama-3-70B excluded for a quantization problem, beam search only expected to work. No MoE.
contradicts_our_findings: No contradiction. Supports 40-50% input sparsity being nearly free in quality for dense models; for the MoE the E.md compute-ceiling argument stands since this paper never tests experts.

title: Forum thread 'Prefill-only requests that consume input tokens without decoding' (OpenAI Developer Community; posted by user dedbot 2026-02-06; one reply by user _j 2026-09-22; closed 2026-09-25)

setup: Not a paper. Feature request: API to create/reuse a prompt cache or prefill state without generating output, for speculative UI branching; motivation: 0.5-1 s time-to-first-token feels sluggish. The reply (a community member with trust level 3, not a moderator/admin, not marked as OpenAI staff) says the feature now exists in the Responses API for gpt-5.6 and later: prompt_cache_options.prewarm = true prepares the cache with no output; the first working breakpoint must be beyond 1024 tokens; also a comparison_response_id diagnostic field. The OpenAI guide (fetched HTML) confirms: 'For GPT-5.6 and later ... Set prompt_cache_options.prewarm to true in a Responses API request to prepare the prompt cache without generating output', with an example of prewarming shared instructions at startup; tokens written during prewarm are billed at the cache-write rate; minimum cacheable prompt 1,024 tokens.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: catalog: 'idea of a precompute-prefix operation is requested as a missing feature; no shipped speculative typing-time prefill found'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: a prewarm operation shipped for GPT-5.6+ (documented in the official guide, not only the forum reply). The shipped feature warms a KNOWN exact prefix (>=1024 tokens); it is not a streaming prefill of a prefix that grows while the user types.

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass: summary 'wrong', reply of Sep 2026 says prewarm now exists
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: confirmed and additionally confirmed in OpenAI's docs page

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass: hosted prefix warm, not typing-time
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: the guide's own example is startup-time prewarm of shared instructions

Relevant to us only as prior art for the user-visible idea (warm before the user submits), not for its mechanism. Note it cannot capture our contribution: ours would prefill the actually-typed partial text in small chunks and pay expert-read cost; the API warms a fixed, complete prefix.

title: A Photonic-CXL Memory Appliance for Scalable KV Cache Management in LLM Inference (Ding, Nishant, Ambati, Kamati, Diep; Marvell Technology). IEEE-style paper, PDF created 2026-07-03
id_read: arXiv 2607.27187 (PDF, 745 text lines; no version label in the PDF)
setup: Part 1, characterisation with vLLM + LMCache: 'repeated request' benchmark (100% hit rate, identical requests), batch sizes {1,2,8,16,32}, prompt lengths 1K-100K (Maverick to 1M, Scout to 4M); models LLaMA-8B (1xA100/H100/H200), LLaMA-70B (2xH200), LLaMA-405B (8xH200, TP=8, BF16), LLaMA Maverick and Scout (MoE, 8xH200). A100 server: PCIe 4.0 x16 (~32 GB/s), 512 GB DRAM, 7 TB local disk; H100/H200 PCIe 5.0 (~64 GB/s), up to 2 TB DRAM. Metric TTFT; speedup = T_compute / T_retrieve. Part 2: Marvell Photonic Fabric memory appliance, 32 TB shared across 16 hosts, 128 GB/s per host; latency emulated on Siemens Veloce Strato-M (350 ns vs 800-900 ns reported for an electrical CXL pool). Part 3: LLMServingSim simulation of LLaMA-405B on 8xH200, multi-turn chat: 10 turns/conversation, 5,120 input + 500 output tokens per turn, 512-token shared system prompt, 50-300 conversations.

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: host-memory speedup of Maverick 2.7x-23.1x and Scout 2.6x-54.6x is below the 405B dense 100x but not below the 8B dense 17.2-27.5x; the authors' own limitations say disk experiments were only done on 8B and 405B, MoE disk was NOT tested

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: the smallest context tested is 1K tokens; for disk at <20K tokens on a GPU server reload is slower than recompute, but that says nothing about a CPU-only laptop where a 500-token prefill takes ~19-21 s (our D.md/E.md numbers)

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass: host memory up to 100x, 6.6x TTFT multi-turn (simulation)
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 100x is 405B on 8xH200 at the longest tested context; 6.6x is simulated, not measured, LLaMA-405B

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass: 50K crossover claim not in abstract, could not verify
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: it IS in the body (Sec II-A3, Table I) - first pass read only the abstract

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass catalog 'wrong' for this row
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: the numbers are right; the catalog's inference to a 500-token reload is the part that is unsupported

why: Server GPUs (A100/H100/H200), PCIe 4/5 at 32-64 GB/s, multi-user datacentre KV pooling with TBs of CXL memory; the 'disk' path is a 7 TB SSD behind PCIe, loaded to GPU HBM. The crossover (disk > recompute only for long contexts) is determined by GPU prefill speed, which is orders of magnitude faster than our CPU prefill (a 500-token prompt = 6e12 FLOP at ~311 GFLOP/s = ~19 s, plus expert I/O), so our break-even is at a few tokens, not 50K. Their formula S = T_compute / T_memory (T_compute ~ 2sP/MFU + attention) makes the dependency explicit; with compute that slow, KV reload wins at any length (D.md P-0153 arithmetic: loading 0.016-0.05 s vs 19-22 s).
ablation: Characterisation varies model, platform, tier (host vs disk), context and batch (Fig 1), which isolates retrieval-vs-recompute; there is no ablation of the appliance beyond the emulation latency.
limitations: Authors: MoE variants and DeepSeek/Qwen only future work (disk tests only 8B and 405B); appliance performance projections come from emulation fed to a simulator, hardware validation pending; single-node.
contradicts_our_findings: Not a contradiction but it corrects how E.md reads this row: E.md says 'disk reload does not pay below about 50K tokens, which we did not test'. The 50K figure is specific to an 8B on A100/H200; on 405B reload wins at all tested lengths, and on our CPU prefill it wins by orders of magnitude (D.md).

title: Speculative Prefill: Turbocharging TTFT with Lightweight and Training-Free Token Importance Estimation (Liu, Chen, Zhang; Univ. of Chicago/Together AI/CMU). arXiv v2, 19 May 2025 (ICML 2025 paper)
setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (BF16) as the speculator picking important prompt chunks via attention scores (look-ahead steps), main model Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct (BF16) or Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct-FP8 receiving only the kept tokens (with original position ids) in vLLM, tensor parallelism 8 on 8xH100/H200 node (efficiency on H200). Quality on LongBench, RULER, short tasks vs LLMLingua, RAG-Llama baselines; token keep rates 10-90%, fixed per task. Efficiency: (1) vLLM server with constant-QPS client on LongBench queries; (2) TTFT vs batch x sequence-length products. Theoretical FLOP model in the appendix (Fig 9: 7.72x predicted vs 7.66x measured at 32K tokens, batch 16).

numbers.value: higher at lower keep rates; lower at higher keep rates (annotated in Fig 9)

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: accurate

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass: up to 7.66x TTFT (405B, 10% keep), Llama-3.1-70B/405B, 8xH100/H200
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: also 7x max QPS

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: first pass: multi-turn needs recompute
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Sec 5: token dropping without explicit context recomputation can fail in multi-turn conversations

why: Lossy prompt-token dropping for long contexts (32K, batch 16) on a GPU node; the 7.66x is a FLOP ratio of the dropped prompt (10% kept), where speculator FLOPs (8B) are small against 405B. On our setup the main model is a 125B MoE with expert I/O dominating prefill (500-token prefill is I/O-bound at 21.4 s), the speculator would itself need a prefill of the whole prompt, and a prompt of ~500 tokens is below the 'long-context' regime in which it pays. It is orthogonal to typing-time prefill (it reduces the work after submit; typing-time prefill hides work before submit) and could in principle be combined, at the cost of quality.
quality_loss: Yes, lossy and task dependent: LongBench/RULER at 10% keep retains most single/multi-doc QA and few-shot quality, degrades summarisation and some RULER tasks (multi-hop tracing at ~400 kept tokens); no single delta number (Table 1, Table 2). Not usable for exact KV.
ablation: Yes: keep-rate sweep 10-90%, with/without look-ahead (Fig 4), versus LLMLingua/RAG baselines, versus MInference TTFT (Fig 5), speculator-size overhead; the cache/I-O dimension is not present.
limitations: Authors: no explicit logits for all input tokens (generative tasks only); multi-turn conversation can fail without recomputing dropped context; fixed keep rate, no adaptive selection yet.

title: LMCache's New Architecture Boosts MoE Inference Performance by 10x (Weishu Deng and the LMCache Team; LMCache Blog, dated 2026-04-03)
id_read: Blog HTML fetched raw with curl and tags stripped (full post read, 9,075 characters of text); no paper, no code run

LMCache MP mode: one shared 400 GB host KV pool (LRU) as a service shared by all ranks. Workload: 'lmcache bench engine --workload multi-round-chat --mrc-qps 2.0 --mrc-duration 120' (2 QPS for 120 s). Single run, no variance, no stated prompt lengths.

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: 3.98/0.29 = 13.7x from the rounded values; the blog itself writes 'approximately 13x' and titles it 10x

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: the gain is specifically from cross-DP-rank sharing: the baseline cannot reuse a prefix cached by another rank

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: single run, LMCache 0.4.3-dev, 2 QPS x 120 s

why: Server multi-tenant prefix reuse across 8 data-parallel ranks, H100s with host RAM pools of 400 GB, comparing shared against unshared per-rank caches; the improvement removes redundant prefill that a shared cache avoids. In a single-user CPU-only laptop there is one process, so there is no cross-rank loss to recover; the part that would transfer is generic 'persist KV across turns' (our D.md session KV rows), where the saving is the whole prefill (19-22 s at 500 tokens). The blog gives no prompt lengths or hit rates, so it cannot be used to size that.
ablation: none (one A/B, shared vs process-local pool; no cache-size or hit-rate breakdown)
limitations: Vendor blog, development build, single configuration, no variance, no hit rate, no prompt-length distribution; roadmap mentions P2P and PD disaggregation not yet available.
